t: Maximize Subarray Sum After Removing All Occurrences of One Element
o: Optionally delete all copies of one value x, then maximize the subarray sum. Deleting x splices the array into 'gaps' between consecutive occurrences of x; the best subarray of the spliced array is a merge of consecutive gaps (partially at the ends, fully in the middle). Naively rebuilding per distinct value is O(D·n). The efficient O(n) method: for each x, fold its gaps left-to-right with a (total, best-prefix, best-suffix, best-subarray) merge — total work is O(n) since gaps across all values partition the array. The answer also includes the untouched Kadane maximum.
k: Removing x turns the array into consecutive gaps; the optimal subarray spans a contiguous run of gaps (partial first/last, full middle ones).
Merging segment summaries (tot, pre, suf, best) with standard formulas combines two adjacent gaps in O(1).
Summed over all distinct values, gap lengths total O(n), so one global pass suffices; the no-op case is covered by plain Kadane.

a.n: Approach 1: Rebuild per distinct value + Kadane
a.i: For each distinct x, filter it out and run Kadane on the remainder. Simple and obviously correct; O(D·n), acceptable when distinct values are few.
s: For each x, build the filtered array and Kadane it
Answer = max over x and the original Kadane
a.t: O(D · n) where D = number of distinct values — degrades to O(n²) when all values differ

a.i: For each value x with occurrence positions, its gaps (runs between consecutive occurrences, plus the two ends) are scanned once to get (tot, pre, suf, best); folding adjacent gaps with merge rules tot=A+B, pre=max(A.pre, A.tot+B.pre), suf=max(B.suf, B.tot+A.suf), best=max(A.best, B.best, A.suf+B.pre) yields the best subarray of the x-free array. Empty gaps are skipped (they merely concatenate neighbors).
s: For each value, iterate its gaps computing per-gap summaries and folding them with the merge rules
Answer = max(global Kadane, all folded bests)
a.t: O(n) — every element belongs to exactly one gap for its own value, so total gap scanning is linear
a.sp: O(n) for the occurrence index lists

w: Why gap merging (not just 'cross one boundary') matters: after deleting x, an optimal subarray may swallow several whole middle gaps (e.g., [1, x, 2, x, 1] → 1+2+1 = 4 beats any single-boundary merge). Verify example 1 gives 7 via x = −2. Use 64-bit sums (values up to 10^6 · 10^5). Edge cases: single-element arrays, all-negative arrays (answer is the max element via Kadane). Follow-up: allow removing occurrences of one value from a subrange, or removing k distinct values — the latter needs segment-tree divide-and-conquer.
